subject: religious-studies
title: Salvation: Augustine, Aquinas, and the Reformers
welcome_lead: Trace the doctrine of salvation from Augustine's controversy with Pelagius to the Reformation debates over justification.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on soteriology: original sin, grace, atonement theories, and justification by faith.
final_note: You have followed Christian soteriology through original sin, the work of Christ, and the means of grace.

concepts.def: The doctrine, articulated by Augustine, that all humanity inherits a fallen condition from Adam.
Disordered desire which Augustine sees as the wound of original sin remaining after baptism.
Grace that goes before, enabling the will to turn toward God.
The view that Christ bore the punishment due to sinners; emphasised by Reformers like Calvin.
The patristic theme, retrieved by Gustaf Aulen, that Christ triumphs over sin, death and Satan.
Latin 'by faith alone'; Luther's principle that justification is by faith without works.

walkthroughs.body_html: Pelagius (c.354-418) taught that humans can choose good without special grace; Adam's sin harmed only Adam. Augustine countered that since the Fall the will is in bondage (non posse non peccare - 'not able not to sin'), and only prevenient grace can liberate it. The Council of Carthage (418) and the Second Council of Orange (529) sided with Augustine.

Aquinas, in Summa Theologiae I-II QQ.109-114, distinguishes operative grace (which heals the will) and cooperative grace (which empowers good acts). He maintains that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it (gratia non tollit naturam sed perficit). Justification involves infused righteousness, not merely imputed.

Luther's breakthrough was reading Romans 1:17: the righteousness of God is not God's punitive justice but a gift given to faith. Justification is by grace alone (sola gratia) through faith alone (sola fide) on account of Christ alone (solus Christus). The Council of Trent (1545-63) replied that justification involves real renewal and condemned the formula of imputation alone.

mcqs.q: What are the main Christian theories of atonement?
options: Atonement means Jesus apologised to humans for being born divine.
All Christians believe Jesus died only to pay God back for sin.

Penal substitution (Christ bore the punishment for sin), Christus Victor (Christ defeated evil powers through the cross), ransom theory (Christ paid a price to free humanity), and moral exemplar (Christ's death inspires love). Different traditions emphasise different theories.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

mcqs.q: What was the Augustine vs Pelagius dispute about original sin?
options: Original sin means Christians believe babies are evil.
Pelagius and Augustine agreed humans are born innocent.

Augustine argued humans inherit a corrupted nature from Adam (original sin) and cannot achieve salvation without grace; Pelagius argued humans retain free will to choose good without divine intervention and that sin is imitated, not inherited.
Atonement means Jesus apologised to humans for being born divine.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Pelagius and Augustine agreed humans are born innocent.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
